newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish president welcomes abortion bill vote.
newsitem.headline: Polish president welcomes abortion bill vote.

text.p: Polish President Aleksander Kwaskniewski on Thursday welcomed a vote by Poland's lower house house of parliament passing a controversial bill relaxing laws on abortion.

"I will sign this law because it is a liberalisation of a very restrictive law that caused a lot of drama," Kwasniewski told Reuters. "I think we should be concentrating on sex education," said the president, who is on an official visit to London.
Deputies in the lower house (Sejm) earlier on Thursday passed the law by 228 votes to 195, overturning a Senate veto.

The new measure allows women to terminate their pregnancies before the 12th week if they face financial or personal problems, provided they undertake counselling and a period of reflection. It also provides for sex education in schools and cheaper contraception.

Kwasniewski, who promised before his election last November that he would support reform of the abortion law passed in 1993 by a pro-Catholic government, has always said he would sign the liberalisation measure.
The new bill was thrown out by the Senate in August, but will now pass into law because the Sejm was able to muster more than the 50 percent plus one votes required.
Kwasniewski was speaking after delivering a speech in which he said integration with the European Union and NATO were Poland's main priorities.
In his speech to the Royal Institute of International Affairs, Kwasniewski said both issues were important for Poland.
"We perceive them as historical opportunities not to be missed," he said.

"The Poles have reached the conclusion that security to them means first of all Poland's membership in the North Atlantic Alliance. Poland is the one country in central Europe where more than 82 percent of the population supports full membership of NATO."

Kwasniewski, a former communist who replaced Solidarity leader Lech Walesa as president last year, argued that enlargement of NATO would strengthen the stability and security of the entire European continent, including Russia.
Kwasniewski received a boost on Tuesday, when U.S. President Bill Clinton used a campaign speech to pledge that NATO would admit new members by 1999.
Kwasniewski stressed that Poland sees itself becoming one of the pillars of NATO, not just an outpost.
"We are confident that Poland's accession to NATO will lead to a projection of stability and security into areas stretching beyond our Eastern frontier."
During his two-day visit, Kwasniewski will holds talks with Prime Minister John Major and opposition leaders and visit Queen Elizabeth.
